44296989.article_content:
Taylor Blau
·
@ttaylorr
June 16, 2025
|
13 minutes
Share:
The open source Git project just
released Git 2.50
with features and bug fixes from 98 contributors, 35 of them new. We last caught up with you on the latest in Git back when
2.49 was released
.
💡 Before we get into the details of this latest release, we wanted to remind you that
Git Merge
, the conference for Git users and developers is back this year on September 29-30, in San Francisco. Git Merge will feature talks from developers working on Git, and in the Git ecosystem. Tickets are on sale now; check out
the website
to learn more.
With that out of the way, let’s take a look at some of the most interesting features and changes from Git 2.50.
Improvements for multiple cruft packs
When we covered
Git 2.43
, we talked about newly added support for
multiple cruft packs
. Git 2.50 improves on that with better command-line ergonomics, and some important bugfixes. In case you’re new to the series, need a refresher, or aren’t familiar with
cruft packs
, here’s a brief overview:
Git
objects
may be either reachable or unreachable. The set of reachable objects is everything you can walk to starting from one of your repository’s
references
: traversing from commits to their parent(s), trees to their sub-tree(s), and so on. Any object that you didn’t visit by repeating that process over all of your references is unreachable.
In
Git 2.37
, Git introduced
cruft packs
, a new way to store your repository’s unreachable objects. A cruft pack looks like an ordinary
packfile
with the addition of an
.mtimes
file, which is used to keep track of when each object was most recently written in order to determine when it is safe
1
to discard it.
However, updating the cruft pack could be cumbersome–particularly in repositories with many unreachable objects–since a repository’s cruft pack must be rewritten in order to add new objects. Git 2.43 began to address this through a new command-line option:
git repack --max-cruft-size
. This option was designed to split unreachable objects across multiple packs, each no larger than the value specified by
--max-cruft-size
. But there were a couple of problems:
If you’re familiar with
git repack
’s
--max-pack-size
option,
--max-cruft-size
’s behavior is quite confusing. The former option specifies the maximum size an individual pack can be, while the latter involves how and when to move objects between multiple packs.
The feature was broken to begin with! Since
--max-cruft-size
also
imposes on cruft packs the same pack-size constraints as
--max-pack-size
does on non-cruft packs, it is often impossible to get the behavior you want.
For example, suppose you had two 100 MiB cruft packs and ran
git repack --max-cruft-size=200M
. You might expect Git to merge them into a single 200 MiB pack. But since
--max-cruft-size
also dictates the maximum size of the output pack, Git will refuse to combine them, or worse: rewrite the same pack repeatedly.
Git 2.50 addresses both of these issues with a new option:
--combine-cruft-below-size
. Instead of specifying the maximum size of the output pack, it determines which existing cruft pack(s) are eligible to be combined. This is particularly helpful for repositories that have accumulated many unreachable objects spread across multiple cruft packs. With this new option, you can gradually reduce the number of cruft packs in your repository over time by combining existing ones together.
With the introduction of
--combine-cruft-below-size
, Git 2.50 repurposed
--max-cruft-size
to behave as a cruft pack-specific override for
--max-pack-size
. Now
--max-cruft-size
only determines the size of the outgoing pack, not which packs get combined into it.
Along the way, a bug was uncovered that prevented objects stored in multiple cruft packs from being “freshened” in
certain circumstances
. In other words, some unreachable objects don’t have their modification times updated when they are rewritten, leading to them being removed from the repository earlier than they otherwise would have been. Git 2.50 squashes this bug, meaning that you can now efficiently manage multiple cruft packs and freshen their objects to your heart’s content.
[
source
,
source
]
Incremental multi-pack reachability bitmaps
​​Back in
our coverage of Git 2.47
, we talked about preliminary support for
incremental multi-pack indexes
. Multi-pack indexes (MIDXs) act like a single pack
*.idx
file for objects spread across multiple packs.
Multi-pack indexes are extremely useful to accelerate object lookup performance in large repositories by binary searching through a single index containing most of your repository’s contents, rather than repeatedly searching through each individual packfile. But multi-pack indexes aren’t just useful for accelerating object lookups. They’re also the basis for multi-pack reachability bitmaps, the MIDX-specific analogue of classic single-pack reachability bitmaps. If neither of those are familiar to you, don’t worry;

data.title: Childhood leukemia: how a deadly cancer became treatable
data.author: surprisetalk
data.article_summary: 这篇文章讨论了儿童白血病的治疗进展，特别是自1970年代以来生存率的大幅提高。过去，儿童白血病的生存率不到10%，但现在北美和欧洲的生存率已达到约85%。文章解释说，白血病是儿童最常见的癌症，尤其以急性淋巴细胞白血病（ALL）和急性髓细胞白血病（AML）为主。虽然有些白血病与遗传有关，但大多数病例是由儿童快速生长过程中自发的基因突变引起的，环境因素的影响尚未明确。通过几十年的研究和临床试验，ALL的五年生存率从1960年代的14%上升到2010年代的94%。AML的生存率也有所提高，但治疗难度较大，改善幅度不如ALL显著。总体而言，现代医学的进步显著提高了儿童白血病的可治性和生存率。
data.comments_summary:

不同观点：
• CobaltFire分享了自己儿子患有B-ALL但通过实验性治疗成功康复的经历，强调了实验性治疗和个性化治疗方案的重要性，同时也指出过长的化疗可能带来的负面影响。
• akharris讲述了自己的父亲作为儿科血液肿瘤学家的经历，表达了对科学进步和临床护理改善的信心，认为未来治愈率将继续提高。
• major505描述了其表弟在20世纪70年代末的巴西通过实验性干扰素治疗白血病成功的故事，并提到其家族因此建立了儿童癌症医院，显示了个人经历对社会贡献的可能性。
• Thomvis则分享了女儿因AML去世的悲痛经历，指出AML的治疗比ALL更加困难，强调了AML异质性和针对性治疗的挑战，但仍对未来的治疗进展抱有希望。
• lysergic回忆了童年好友因白血病去世的经历，批评了当时治疗的副作用和无效性，并指出了治疗对患者及其家庭的深远影响。
• rglover作为ALL的幸存者，强调了长期治疗对个人生活的深远影响，并希望更多孩子能获得负担得起的治疗。
• robwwilliams批评了文章对治疗进展解释的不清晰，强调了个体化治疗和基因分型在治疗中的重要性。
• khelavastr提出需要研究白血病发病率的变化，质疑是否某些群体现在得到了更多可治疗的版本。
• cloin分享了自己孩子即将完成B-ALL治疗的经历，强调了医疗团队的准备和应对能力。
• bglazer介绍了20世纪60年代Don Pinkel在St. Jude开发组合治疗的先锋工作，强调了早期研究对提高治愈率的贡献。
• Zaylan对比了过去和现在白血病生存率的变化，指出科学进步的显著性，但仍关注全球范围内的治疗可及性问题。
• find通过数据分析指出，现代儿童认识的白血病患者死亡率显著降低，显示了治疗进展对社会的整体影响。
• Vinnl赞扬了为治疗进展做出贡献的各方，强调了每一个小进步对整体社会的价值。
• l-survivor作为ALL幸存者，分享了治疗对个人和学业的长远影响，并关注到家庭在治疗过程中承受的负担。
• thinkcontext呼吁更多人加入骨髓捐献者登记，强调了骨髓移植对某些白血病患者的重要性，并分享了个人作为捐献者的经历和感受。

补充讨论：
• 讨论中多次提到个性化治疗和实验性治疗的重要性，特别是对不同类型白血病的针对性治疗。
• 医疗团队的准备和应对能力被多次提及，显示了医疗支持在治疗过程中的关键作用。
• 骨髓捐献者登记和全球治疗可及性问题也是讨论中的重要议题，显示了社会支持和全球医疗公平性的必要性。

44282143.article_content:
Home
Cancer
In the past, when I’d hear the words childhood leukemia, I’d picture a young child who suddenly became seriously ill, and whose parents were told their child had only a few years to live.
I’d wonder how a child might grasp the idea of limited time, or how painful it must have been to face the possibility of missing out on growing up, discovering who they are, and forming deep friendships. It would also be a tragic experience for their family, friends, and classmates, who might struggle to understand what’s happening.
This picture, reflected in films, books, and television, depicts what used to be a grim reality. Childhood leukemia was fatal for the vast majority of children who developed it in the past. Before the 1970s, fewer than 10% of children diagnosed with the disease survived five years after diagnosis.
But since then, this outlook has improved dramatically. In North America and Europe, around 85% now survive that long.
1
What made this dramatic change possible? In this article, I’ll describe the progress achieved and some concrete reasons behind it.
This article focuses on data from North America and Europe; death rates from childhood cancers have also
declined in other world regions
, but remain higher.
Leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, and its mortality rates have been reduced substantially
Many different types of cancer can affect children. This article focuses on leukemia, the most common type of childhood cancer.
In the chart below, you can see the reduction in cancer death rates in the United States among children of different ages. The decline has been particularly large for leukemia, with a 14-fold drop, but we’ve also made much progress on
other, less common childhood cancers
.
Download image
Explore the data for other countries in
an interactive chart
.
Leukemia is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow — the tissue that produces blood cells. It develops when immature white blood cells grow out of control and crowd out healthy ones, leading to symptoms like fatigue, infections, easy bruising or bleeding, and pale skin.
While leukemia becomes more common with age, it’s the most frequent cancer in children, making up about a quarter of all childhood cancer cases in the United States.
2
One reason may be that blood-forming tissues are especially active during childhood, when the body grows quickly and needs a steady supply of new blood cells to carry oxygen, fight infections, and form clots. Many of these cells also have short lifespans, and this stage of life is a crucial period for immune system development.
3
This is very demanding for the bone marrow, which must constantly produce new cells. Each time a cell divides, there’s a small chance of a DNA error, and the more divisions that occur, the greater the chance that some of these errors will lead to cancer.
There are two main types of leukemia in children. The most common is
acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
, which starts in early lymphoid cells. The other is
acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
, which begins in other blood-forming cells.
4
Most childhood leukemia cases result from genetic mutations that develop spontaneously during this rapid cell division, often occurring before birth, while others are due to inherited genetic mutations, which are less common.
5
While several environmental exposures have been investigated, there hasnʼt been consistent evidence for any environmental causes.
6
Childhood leukemia has become much more treatable
Survival rates for children with leukemia have risen dramatically in the last 50 years.
The chart below plots overall survival rates — the share of children still alive after a given time since their diagnosis. The data comes from trials by the Children’s Oncology Group, which has enrolled tens of thousands of children since the 1960s, and now includes over half of all children with leukemia in the US.
7
The top panel displays this for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) while the bottom panel shows acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
In the top panel, you can see that in the 1960s, only around 14% of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia survived at least five years. Despite initially improving upon treatment, most relapsed and died soon after.
By the 2010s, the chances of survival had increased dramatically: 94% of children survived at least five years.

After the initial years of treatment, their long-term survival is much more stable.

44282143.article_summary: 这篇文章讨论了儿童白血病的治疗进展，特别是自1970年代以来生存率的大幅提高。过去，儿童白血病的生存率不到10%，但现在北美和欧洲的生存率已达到约85%。文章解释说，白血病是儿童最常见的癌症，尤其以急性淋巴细胞白血病（ALL）和急性髓细胞白血病（AML）为主。虽然有些白血病与遗传有关，但大多数病例是由儿童快速生长过程中自发的基因突变引起的，环境因素的影响尚未明确。通过几十年的研究和临床试验，ALL的五年生存率从1960年代的14%上升到2010年代的94%。AML的生存率也有所提高，但治疗难度较大，改善幅度不如ALL显著。总体而言，现代医学的进步显著提高了儿童白血病的可治性和生存率。

主要讨论点：世界最小电机的历史背景及其技术意义，以及对更大规模微电机的商业应用探讨。

不同观点：
• [kens] 认为1959年Feynman的演讲奠定了纳米技术领域的基础，并介绍了Feynman为推动微型工具发展而设立的奖项。虽然有人迅速赢得了奖金，但该电机并没有带来新的技术突破或推动纳米技术的发展。直到1985年，Feynman的第二个挑战——将一页文本缩小25,000倍——才被完成。这表明微型电机早期发展的局限性。

• [chaosprint] 对微型电机在商业产品中的应用更感兴趣，特别是类似于智能旋钮（smartknob）的大规模生产的可行性，询问是否已有可量产的微电机产品。

• [blutack] 提供了有关一家公司曾生产手动浓缩咖啡机的例子，但不确定该产品在Kickstarter众筹活动后是否继续生产，暗示微型电机技术在消费品中的应用可能面临生产持续性的问题。

补充讨论：
• Feynman的奖项激励虽然促进了微型电机的发展，但早期成果并未直接推动纳米技术的进步。
• 讨论中提到了微型电机在消费电子和智能设备中的潜在应用，如智能旋钮，以及这些技术从众筹项目到持续生产的挑战。
• 链接提供了有关Feynman演讲和微型技术挑战的更多详细信息，供进一步阅读。

争议焦点：早期微型电机技术是否真正推动了纳米技术的发展，或者仅仅是在尺寸上取得了突破而缺乏实际技术创新。

data.title: Should we design for iffy internet?
data.author: surprisetalk
data.article_summary: 文章讨论了2025年美国仍有部分家庭互联网连接不稳定，呼吁软件开发者不应默认用户都有高速网络，需优化数据传输量。作者引用了联邦通信委员会（FCC）和国家教育统计中心（NCES）的数据，指出约97%的美国家庭能接入互联网，但网速通常不超过25Mbps下载和3Mbps上传，且延迟可能较高。城市地区网络较好，而农村地区较差。文章建议，在设计软件时需考虑网络不佳的用户，尤其是在面向消费者（B2C）的应用中。尽管商业可得性地图显示广泛覆盖，但市场渗透率数据不明，因此需根据具体用户群体决定设计策略。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：互联网连接质量对网站和应用设计的影响，尤其是在低带宽、高延迟和不稳定连接环境下的用户体验问题。

不同观点：
• [AnotherGoodName] 指出，尽管网站通常可以在25Mbps下行和3Mbps上行的速度下正常工作，但对于依赖旧卫星网络（如太平洋岛屿）的用户，网速极低且不稳定，网站往往无法加载。Starlink为这些社区带来了革命性变化，但尚未覆盖所有地区。
• [zeinhajjali] 强调，在研究“数字鸿沟”时，公共数据的质量问题使得准确绘制这一现象变得困难。不同数据集的形状和格式不一致，导致分析过程中丢失细节。
• [DannyPage] 认为，城市地区的移动互联网丢包问题同样严重，即使在技术上在线，实际体验却常常离线，例如在地铁中使用Spotify的糟糕体验。
• [Sanzig] 指出，现代网页应用对延迟敏感，尤其是在高延迟环境下（如航班WiFi）。开发者在低延迟环境下工作时往往忽视优化，建议使用网络模拟工具进行基本可用性测试。
• [nine_k] 分享了在工作中通过设计API和前端加载优化，解决不稳定互联网连接问题的经验，强调了实际测试的重要性。
• [Workaccount2] 提出，是否应为满足少数用户而对产品进行大量优化是一个长期争论的问题，不同人有不同的限度。
• [potatolicious] 补充，大多数用户通过移动设备和无线连接访问网站，网速和延迟变化很大，需要更多关注。
• [morleytj] 支持简化网站设计，指出在高延迟环境下，简单HTML页面表现更好。
• [jazzyjackson] 指出共享WiFi环境下的问题，如咖啡馆和学生工作场所，路由器客户端轮换服务导致连接不稳定。
• [mlhpdx] 分享了个人经历，住在低密度社区，尽管富裕但互联网基础设施老旧，面临选择高延迟高带宽（Starlink）或低延迟低带宽（DSL）的困境。
• [cjs_ac] 回忆早期互联网使用经历，强调优化请求和响应的重要性。
• [gadders] 批评某些应用花费过长时间判断网络状态，即使它们可以在离线状态下工作。
• [neepi] 担心未来互联网连接的不确定性，主张为离线工作进行设计以应对风险。
• [jebarker] 认为，设计应考虑低端硬件和低速连接，以提升所有用户的体验。
• [dghlsakjg] 强烈建议设计时考虑最坏情况，确保在1Mbps连接和频繁中断情况下仍能正常使用。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点之一是是否应为满足少数极端情况（如极低带宽和高延迟环境）而对所有用户体验进行优化。部分人认为应设计为满足大多数用户，而另一些人则认为优化对所有用户都有益。
• 另一个值得注意的点是，公共数据质量问题在研究数字鸿沟时带来的挑战，数据不一致导致难以准确分析问题。
• 开发者在低延迟环境下工作时往往忽视高延迟用户的体验，建议使用网络模拟工具进行测试以发现问题。

总的来说，讨论围绕如何在不同网络环境下优化网站和应用的用户体验，强调了考虑极端情况和进行实际测试的重要性。

44298656.article_content:
Should we design for iffy internet?
Brian Hicks, June 16, 2025
I keep hearing claims like this:
Not everyone in the US has access to stable, reliable internet, even in 2025.
Web developers should stop assuming people have fast internet connections and slim their payloads accordingly.
This seems intuitively true to meâprogrammers are gonna have better connectivity because that takes money, and programmers are well-paid. But what's the actual scope of the problem?
I dug around, and here's some data. My goal here is not to beat anyone over the head with "THOU SHALT NOT ASSUME GOOD INTERNET" but to give an idea about the scope of broadband rollout in the US in a way that can help inform choices we make when designing software.
If you don't feel like reading this whole thing, here's the bottom line up front:
you can probably assume internet access in somewhere around 97% of US households, but you should not assume that it's better than around 25Mbps down and 3Mbps up, and latency may be significantly worse than you previously assumed. This is likely worse for B2C software than B2B.
I'm going to pull from two US government agencies here: the
Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
and the
National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)
(part of the Department of Education.) All the data I'm referencing was published well before the current administration started gutting the bureaucracy, so I think it's fairly reliable.
Assumptions
Before we begin, there are a bunch of ways to define "stable" or "reliable" internet connections. For the purposes of this post, I'm defining that as a
terrestrial link with at least 25Mbps down and 3Mbps up.
Terrestrial becauseâwell, have you ever tried to use a satellite connection for anything real? Latency is awful, and the systems tend to go down in bad weather. They also have had fairly low data caps historically so you had to use your connection judiciously, although this may be changing.
1
2
25/3Mpbs because that's a fairly common cable package speed, and also around the minimum Iâve been able to use modern SaaS apps on without it getting ridiculously frustrating.
Zoom says
you need 1â4 Mbps in both directions to do a video call.
The FCC's broadband map lets you set both these criteria. Let's have a look at it.
The FCC Broadband Map
The FCC tracks access to broadband internet in the US. As a result, they publish a map that's more accurate than the maps you see from ISPs. This isn't
completely
error-free, but individuals and companies can both submit data on coverage at a street address level and challenge inaccuracies in the existing data. For our purposes, I think it's good enough!
I'm going to grab some screenshots of the map to fix it at the current data for discussion. That way we can get an idea about regional coverage.
Strangely, they don't let you zoom out enough to grab a screenshot of the whole country so I'm going to look at the west. That'll get both urban and rural coverage, as well as several famously internet-y locations (San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle.)
If you want to follow along or compare how the data has changed since this post was published, you can get the map yourself at
broadbandmap.fcc.gov
.
First, here's a hex map of coverage using the criteria we set above. The darker each hex is, the higher the percent coverage within it. Dark blue is 100%, white is 0%, grays or faded blues are in between.
This shows pretty much what I'd expect: coverage is fine in and around cities and less great in rural areas.
3
(The Dakotas are an interesting exception;
there's a co-op up there
that connected a ton of folks with gigabit fiber. Pretty cool!)
Although, remember that these are
minimum
criteria. When I'm building software, I'm mostly doing it on my home internet. A test just now says I get 367/71Mpbs. What does the country look like if I were to expect all my users to have similar connections? The map lets us filter for 250/25; let's look:
Cities are pretty much unchanged, but rural coverage gets much worse. (Except again for North Dakota, the reigning champion of rural fiber.)
So what does this tell us about how we should design software? One big takeaway: if you design for the
availability
of fast internet connections, you'll exclude many people in rural areas.
This may or may not be OK for your marketâ"good internet" tends to be in population centers, and population centers tend to contain more businesses and consumers. You have to make that call!
However, it's also worth keeping in mind that this is a map of commercial availability, not market penetration. Hypothetically, you could get the average speed of a US residential internet connection, but the FCC doesn't make such a statistic available.
4
However, we have another source of data!
Student Internet Access
The US Department of Education occasionally tracks student internet access. Since classwork and homework have moved more online (especially during the early days of COVID) it's useful data for pol

• [mlhpdx] 分享了个人经历，住在低密度社区，尽管富裕但互联网基础设施老旧，面临选择高延迟高带宽（Starlink）或低延迟低带宽（DSL）的困境。
• [cjs_ac] 回忆早期互联网使用经历，强调优化请求和响应的重要性。
• [gadders] 批评某些应用花费过长时间判断网络状态，即使它们可以在离线状态下工作。
• [neepi] 担心未来互联网连接的不确定性，主张为离线工作进行设计以应对风险。
• [jebarker] 认为，设计应考虑低端硬件和低速连接，以提升所有用户的体验。
• [dghlsakjg] 强烈建议设计时考虑最坏情况，确保在1Mbps连接和频繁中断情况下仍能正常使用。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点之一是是否应为满足少数极端情况（如极低带宽和高延迟环境）而对所有用户体验进行优化。部分人认为应设计为满足大多数用户，而另一些人则认为优化对所有用户都有益。
• 另一个值得注意的点是，公共数据质量问题在研究数字鸿沟时带来的挑战，数据不一致导致难以准确分析问题。
• 开发者在低延迟环境下工作时往往忽视高延迟用户的体验，建议使用网络模拟工具进行测试以发现问题。

总的来说，讨论围绕如何在不同网络环境下优化网站和应用的用户体验，强调了考虑极端情况和进行实际测试的重要性。

data.title: The Collapse of Complex Societies
data.author: giraffe_lady
data.article_summary:
这篇文章讨论了对所谓“AI末日论”的批评，并指出这种担忧其实源于几十年前就存在的技术末日论传统。文章回顾了1972年出版的《增长的极限》一书，该书通过模型预测，若全球人口、工业化、污染、粮食生产和资源消耗等五大因素不加改变，地球将在未来一百年内达到增长极限，导致人口和工业能力急剧下降。该书的预测方法和结论曾引发争议，后续更新研究仍得出类似结果。

文章还介绍了1988年约瑟夫·泰恩特所著《复杂社会的崩溃》一书，泰恩特认为社会复杂性的增加会导致边际回报递减，最终复杂社会将因维持现状的成本过高而崩溃。这与《增长的极限》的预测相呼应，提出了当前社会是否正在接近崩溃的问题。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：社会崩溃的可能性及其预测模型的有效性

不同观点：
• **myflash13** 认为社会不一定因为某个节点而彻底结束，但生活质量会持续恶化，尤其是在西方国家。他以千禧一代的经济状况为例，指出大多数人生活状况不如父母，只有少数移居其他地区的人例外。

• **gweinberg** 对预测社会崩溃的模型持怀疑态度。他认为这些模型虽然看似 robust（坚固），但其基本假设存在高度可疑之处，因为无论如何调整参数，最终都会得出崩溃的结论，只是时间问题。

• **Isamu** 指出，批评“AI 末日论者”的人往往忽视了技术末日论有着几十年的知识传统。他质疑像《增长的极限》这类模型中的数学假设，认为其曲线选择是随意的，缺乏实证依据。此外，他认为“崩溃”一词被广泛滥用，导致讨论变得模糊和夸张。

• **gmuslera** 用“囚徒困境”类比全球社会动态，指出所有参与者都朝着墙加速前进，任何一方试图减速都会被其他方损害。因此，在这种系统中，重新定义“理性行动”变得至关重要。

• **vdupras** 提出，人类社会依赖于复杂的承诺网络。这些承诺层层叠加，互相利用。未来的承诺已经被大量预支，任何试图解决这些承诺的人都会发现大规模的承诺破灭不可避免，这将导致社会资源缩减、冲突增加，最终可能引发崩溃。

补充讨论：
- 对“崩溃”一词的定义和使用存在争议，Isamu 认为其过于模糊和夸张，影响了理性讨论。
- 模型的基本假设和预测的有效性是争议焦点，gweinberg 和 Isamu 都对其持怀疑态度。
- 讨论中涉及了系统动态、囚徒困境等复杂系统理论，表明社会崩溃可能不仅仅是经济问题，还涉及社会结构和决策理性。

foreÂ­told.
Of course, predicÂ­tions of global apocÂ­aÂ­lypse are as ancient as humanity. Given the historÂ­ical track recordâ
no global apocÂ­aÂ­lypse yet!
âthose predicting apocÂ­aÂ­lypse have tradiÂ­tionÂ­ally had a rough time being taken seriÂ­ously. Still, there is a big differÂ­ence between predicting the arrival of apocÂ­aÂ­lypse
ex nihilo
vs. a reasoned arguÂ­ment that it necesÂ­sarily emerges from specific human deciÂ­sions and
habits.
The Limits of Growth
This book, published in 1972, was an early effort to quanÂ­tiÂ­taÂ­tively model the effects of techÂ­noÂ­logÂ­ical change. I read it some years ago. As the title implies,
The Limits of Growth
considÂ­ered how
five key global factors
would affect human
develÂ­opÂ­ment:
If the present growth trends in world popuÂ­laÂ­tion, indusÂ­triÂ­alÂ­izaÂ­tion, polluÂ­tion, food producÂ­tion, and resource depleÂ­tion continue unchanged, the limits to growth on this planet will be reached someÂ­time within the next one hundred years. The most probÂ­able result will be a rather
sudden and unconÂ­trolÂ­lable decline in both popuÂ­laÂ­tion and indusÂ­trial capacity
.
In support of their theoÂ­ries, and unusuÂ­ally for the era, the authors of TLoG relied extenÂ­sively on softÂ­ware simuÂ­laÂ­tions. This allowed the authors to, say, model the course of human progress under realÂ­istic current assumpÂ­tions. In this model, popuÂ­laÂ­tion decreases rapidly after aroundÂ
2050:
But using a softÂ­ware model also allowed the authors to run simuÂ­laÂ­tions with different starting assumpÂ­tions, such as this one with natural resources doubled. Perhaps counÂ­terÂ­inÂ­tuÂ­itively, the model predicts that increasing resources causes the big drop in popuÂ­laÂ­tion to happen
sooner
because unconÂ­trolled polluÂ­tion negates the beneÂ­fits of the extra
resources:
For 1972, these charts are pretty rad. They remind me of output from programs in my beloved childÂ­hood copy of
BASIC Computer Games
.
ConsisÂ­tent with the usual historÂ­ical reacÂ­tion to doomers, TLoGâs methods and concluÂ­sions were diviÂ­sive for decades. The origÂ­inal authors produced multiple sequels:
Beyond the Limits
in 1992,
Limits to Growth: the 30-Year Update
in 2004, and
Limits and Beyond
in 2022. Spoiler: the popuÂ­laÂ­tion still collapses. In the 2023 paper
RecalÂ­iÂ­braÂ­tion of Limits to Growth
, a sepaÂ­rate group of authors ran the TLoG simuÂ­laÂ­tions with updated empirÂ­ical data. Result? You guessedÂ
it.
The Collapse of Complex Societies
ThisÂ
1988 book
, by
Joseph Tainter
, I read earlier this year. I recomÂ­mend itâas a work of suspenseful persuaÂ­sive writing, itâs pretty great. (For those who prefer to preserve the suspense: itâs safe to read this section, but skip
the last one
.)
Tainter is an anthroÂ­polÂ­oÂ­gist. His defiÂ­nÂ­iÂ­tion of collapse is similar to that of TLoG: âa rapid, signifÂ­iÂ­cant loss of an estabÂ­lished level of sociopoÂ­litÂ­ical complexity.â It doesnât mean the end of a society, necesÂ­sarily. Rather, it marks a point after which quality of life tends to get ever worse for ever more
people.
But the primary quesÂ­tion posed by the book is never said out loud till near the end: is our own society approaching a state of collapse? Might it already be
happening?
In contrast to TLoG, Tainter considers collapse retroÂ­specÂ­tively rather than prospecÂ­tively. Even though complex sociÂ­eties have only existed for a small fracÂ­tion of human history, Tainter observes that theyâve neverÂ­theÂ­less displayed a strong propenÂ­sity toward collapse.Â
Why?
Tainterâs theory is straightÂ­forÂ­ward. First, he notes that sociopoÂ­litÂ­ical complexity incurs costs, and that increasing complexity imposes increasing costs. Second, he observes that econÂ­oÂ­mists have shown that the prinÂ­ciple of diminÂ­ishing returns is one of the best evidenced in human historyânearly an iron law. Putting these together, Tainter theoÂ­rizes that sociÂ­eties grow more complex
until:
â¦Â the increased costs of sociopoÂ­litÂ­ical evoluÂ­tion â¦Â reach a point of diminÂ­ishing marginal returns. â¦Â After a certain point, increased investÂ­ments in complexity fail to yield proporÂ­tionÂ­ately increasing returns. Marginal returns decline and marginal costs rise. Complexity as a strategy becomes increasÂ­ingly costly, and yields decreasing marginal
beneÂ­fits.
Or more colloÂ­quiÂ­allyâluxury becomes necesÂ­sity. Complex sociÂ­eties are thereby forced into a posiÂ­tion where an increasing share of their social resources are spent mainÂ­taining the status quo rather than investing in future

data.title: Rules, Not Renewables, Might Explain the Iberian Blackout
data.author: rbanffy
data.article_summary: 文章讨论了2021年发生在伊比利亚半岛的大规模停电事件，指出停电原因可能并非可再生能源问题，而是电网管理规则不足。作者认为，未来的电网需要更好地激励和管理无功功率，以维持电力系统的稳定性。无功功率在电压控制中起关键作用，而当前的规则和激励措施可能不足以应对可再生能源接入带来的挑战。文章强调，改进电网管理和规则制定比单纯增加可再生能源容量更为重要，以防止类似停电事件再次发生。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：可再生能源在电网中的技术问题及责任归属

不同观点：
• **cogman10的观点**：可再生能源在电网中的“孤岛化”问题（renewable islanding）是一个技术问题，而不是规则问题。可再生能源不愿成为无功功率源，当频率下降时，它们往往会切断电源以避免对电网和其他电力供应商造成损害。相比之下，传统的旋转圆盘电源供应商具有动量，能够承受低电压并自我纠正，而可再生能源缺乏这种能力。因此，解决办法是制定针对可再生能源生产者的规则，要求安装必要的孤岛设备，而不是简单地切断电源。

• **diggan的观点**：目前关于电网故障原因的讨论为时尚早。引用了西班牙电网运营商REE误算导致大规模停电的事件，并指出官方调查尚未得出结论，预计需要数月时间才能发布报告。diggan认为在官方结论发布之前，进行原因猜测和争论没有太大意义。

• **ErneX的观点**：指出能源结构已经发生变化，增加了更多联合循环发电（combined cycle），这可能暗示了问题的根源所在，即能源结构的变化可能影响了电网的稳定性。

• **MaxHoppersGhost的观点**：认为欧洲调查者不可能将责任归咎于可再生能源，暗示可能存在对可再生能源的偏见或保护。

补充讨论：
• **jakub_g的观点**：提到相关的平行讨论，即西班牙电网运营商的误算导致了大规模停电，进一步指出在缺乏官方结论的情况下进行猜测和讨论可能不准确。
• 争议焦点在于可再生能源在电网故障中的责任问题，一部分人认为技术问题是主要原因，而另一部分人则认为在官方调查结果发布前进行猜测没有意义，还有人暗示对可再生能源的偏见。

data.title: What I Wish Someone Told Me When I Was Getting into ARIA
data.author: todsacerdoti
data.article_summary: 本文简要介绍了ARIA（可访问富互联网应用程序）的概念及其在网页可访问性中的作用。ARIA为HTML标记提供额外信息，帮助屏幕阅读器和语音控制软件更好地理解网页内容。它用于描述交互性、目的和状态，例如按钮是否被激活或折叠面板的当前状态。ARIA并非一本如何构建无障碍网站的指南，而是帮助设计和开发人员正确理解和使用ARIA的思维框架。文章还回顾了ARIA的历史和发展，指出其初版发布于2006年，最新版为2023年的1.2版本，并简要提及了其未来发展。作者强调，ARIA是HTML局限性的补充，使用时需谨慎，以避免误用带来的问题。

• **[rhdunn] 支持使用 ARIA 作者实践指南 (APG)**：rhdunn 认为 ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) 是其实现自定义元素时的重要参考，因为该指南清晰规定了给定元素在特定状态下的键盘导航、ARIA 角色、状态和属性的要求，比直接阅读核心规范更易于实施和测试。

• **[askew] 强调谨慎使用 ARIA，避免滥用**：askew 同意 ARIA 可以在将不规范的 "div 汤"（指 HTML 结构混乱的页面）转化为更具可访问性的元素方面发挥重要作用，但指出像文章中提到的，随意使用 `aria-label` 并不会自动使界面可访问，反而可能带来意外的负面效果。

• **[nailer] 认为 ARIA 是“釜底抽薪”式的解决方案，主张通过计算机视觉模型替代**：nailer 认为 ARIA 只是帮助了无障碍行业，但并不是解决问题的最佳方式。他提出，更好的解决方案是通过专注于无障碍的计算机视觉模型来解决可访问性问题。

补充讨论：
• **ARIA 的有效性和使用限制**：评论中讨论了 ARIA 的优势和潜在问题，特别是如果使用不当（如滥用 `aria-label`），可能会产生负面影响。
• **技术替代方案的讨论**：nailer 提出了使用计算机视觉模型作为 ARIA 的替代方案，这引出了关于未来无障碍技术发展方向的讨论。
• **争议焦点**：ARIA 是否是解决可访问性问题的最佳工具，尤其是在有其他技术（如计算机视觉模型）可以选择的情况下。

Eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs.

Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA)
is an inevitability when working on web accessibility. That said, it’s everyone’s first time learning about ARIA at some point.
If you haven’t encountered ARIA before, great! It’s a chance to learn something new and exciting. If you have heard of ARIA before, this might help you better understand it or maybe even teach you something new!
These are all things I wish someone had told me when I was getting started on my web accessibility journey. This post will:
Provide a mindset for
how to approach ARIA
as a concept,
Debunk some common misconceptions
, and
Provide some guiding thoughts
to help you better understand and work with it.
It is my hope that in doing so, this post will help make an oft-overlooked yet vital corner of web design and development easier to approach.
What This Post Is Not
This
is not
a recipe book for how to use ARIA to build accessible websites and web apps. It is also not a guide for how to remediate an inaccessible experience.
A lot of accessibility work is highly contextual
. I do not know the specific needs of your project or organization, so trying to give advice here could easily do more harm than good.
Instead, think of this post as a “know before you go” guide. I’m hoping to give you a good headspace to approach ARIA, as well as highlight things to watch out for when you undertake your journey. So, with that out of the way, let’s dive in!
Roll up your sleeves and
boost your UX skills
! Meet
Smart Interface Design Patterns
🍣, a 10h video library by Vitaly Friedman.
100s of real-life examples
and live UX training.
Free preview
.
Jump to table of contents ↬
So, What Is ARIA?
ARIA is what you turn to if there is not a native HTML element or attribute that is better suited for the job of communicating interactivity, purpose, and state.
Think of it like a spice that you sprinkle into your markup to enhance things.
Adding ARIA to your HTML markup is a way of providing additional information to a website or web app for
screen readers
and
voice control software
.
Interactivity
means the content can be activated or manipulated. An example of this is navigating to a link’s destination.
Purpose
means what something is used for. An example of this is a text input used to collect someone’s name.
State
means the current status content has been placed in and controlled by
states, properties, and values
. An example of this is an accordion panel ​​that can either be expanded or collapsed.
Here is an illustration to help communicate what I mean by this:
(
Large preview
)
The presence of
HTML’s
button
element
will instruct assistive technology to report it as a button, letting someone know that it can be activated to perform a predefined action.
The presence of the text string “Mute” will be reported by assistive technology to clue the person into what the button is used for.
The presence of
aria-pressed="true"
means that someone or something has previously activated the button, and it is now in a “pushed in” state that sustains its action.
This overall pattern will let people who use assistive technology know:
If something is interactive,
What kind of interactive behavior it performs, and
Its
current state
.
ARIA’s History
ARIA has been around for a long time, with
the first version published on September 26th, 2006
.
(
Large preview
)
ARIA was created to provide a bridge between the limitations of HTML and the need for making interactive experiences understandable by assistive technology.
“
The latest version of ARIA is
version 1.2
, published on June 6th, 2023. Version 1.3 is slated to be released relatively soon, and you can read more about it in
this excellent article by Craig Abbott
.
You may also see it referred to as WAI-ARIA, where WAI stands for “Web Accessibility Initiative.” The
WAI
is part of the
W3C
, the organization that sets standards for the web. That said, most accessibility practitioners I know call it “ARIA” in written and verbal communication and leave out the “WAI-” part.
The Spirit Of ARIA Reflects The Era In Which It Was Created
The reason for this is simple: The web was a lot less mature in the past than it is now. The most popular operating system in 2006 was
Windows XP
. The iPhone didn’t exist yet; it was released a year later.
From a very high level,
ARIA is a snapshot of the operating system interaction paradigms of this time period
. This is bec
44299930.article_summary: 本文简要介绍了ARIA（可访问富互联网应用程序）的概念及其在网页可访问性中的作用。ARIA为HTML标记提供额外信息，帮助屏幕阅读器和语音控制软件更好地理解网页内容。它用于描述交互性、目的和状态，例如按钮是否被激活或折叠面板的当前状态。ARIA并非一本如何构建无障碍网站的指南，而是帮助设计和开发人员正确理解和使用ARIA的思维框架。文章还回顾了ARIA的历史和发展，指出其初版发布于2006年，最新版为2023年的1.2版本，并简要提及了其未来发展。作者强调，ARIA是HTML局限性的补充，使用时需谨慎，以避免误用带来的问题。

Preston's story highlights the power of hard work and second chances, inspiring others facing similar challenges.

44288937.article_content:
Jun 16, 2025
Working on databases from prison: How I got here, part 2.
Preston Thorpe
I'm very excited to announce that I have recently joined Turso as a software engineer. For many in the field, including myself, getting to work on databases and solve unique challenges with such a talented team would be a dream job, but it is that much more special to me because of my unusual and unlikely circumstances. As difficult as it might be to believe, I am currently incarcerated and I landed this job from my cell in state prison. If you don’t know me, let me tell you more about how I got here.
#
How I got here
Nearly two years have passed since I published
How I got here
to my blog. That post was my first real contact with the outside world in years, as I'd been off all social media and the internet since 2017. The response and support I would receive from the tech community caught me completely off guard.
A brief summary is that I'm currently serving prison time for poor decisions and lifestyle choices I made in my twenties, all related to drugs. Three years ago, I enrolled in a prison college program that came with the unique opportunity to access a computer with limited internet access. This immediately reignited a teenage love for programming and a lightbulb immediately lit up: that this would be my way out of the mess I had gotten myself into over the past 15 years. I quickly outgrew the curriculum, preferring instead to spend ~15+ hours a day on projects and open source contributions.
Through fortunate timing and lots of hard work, I was selected to be one of the first participants in the Maine Dept of Correction’s remote work program, where residents who meet certain requirements are allowed to seek out remote employment opportunities. I landed a software engineering job at a startup called
Unlocked Labs
building education solutions for incarcerated learners, while contributing to open source on the side. After just a year, I was leading their development team.
#
Finding Turso: hacking on project Limbo
Last December I was between side-projects and browsing Hacker News when I discovered Project Limbo, an effort by Turso to rewrite SQLite from scratch. I'd never worked on relational databases, but some experience with a cache had recently sparked an interest in storage engines. Luckily for me I saw that the project was fairly young with plenty of low hanging fruit to cut my teeth on.
To put this entirely into perspective for some of you may be difficult, but in prison there isn’t exactly a whole lot to do and programming
absolutely
consumes my life. I either write code or manage Kubernetes clusters or other infrastructure for about 90 hours a week, and my only entertainment is a daily hour of tech/programming YouTube; mostly consisting of The Primeagen, whose story was a huge inspiration to me early on.
Through Prime, I had known about Turso since the beginning and had watched several interviews with Glauber and Pekka discussing their Linux kernel backgrounds and talking about the concept of distributed, multi-tenant SQLite. These were folks I'd looked up to for years and definitely could not have imagined that I would eventually be in any position to be contributing meaningfully to such an ambitious project of theirs. So needless to say, for those first PR's, just the thought of a kernel maintainer reviewing my code had made me quite nervous.
Helping build Limbo quickly became my new obsession. I split my time between my job and diving deep into SQLite source code, academic papers on database internals, and Andy Pavlo's CMU lectures. I was active on the
Turso Discord
but I don't think I considered whether anyone was aware that one of the top contributors was doing so from a prison cell. My story and information are linked on my GitHub, but it's subtle enough where you could miss it if you didn't read the whole profile. A couple months later, I got a Discord message from Glauber introducing himself and asking if we could meet.
In January, Glauber's
tweet
about our interaction caught the attention of The Primeagen, and he ended up
reading my blog post
on his stream, bringing a whole lot of new attention to it.
To this day I receive semi-regular emails either from developers, college kids or others who maybe have either gone through addiction or similar circumstances, or just want to reach out for advice on how to best start contributing to open source or optimize their learning path.
#
What's Next
I'm incredibly proud to be an example to others of how far hard work, determination and discipline will get you, and will be forever grateful for the opportunities given to me by the Maine Dept of Corrections to even be able to work hard in the first place, and to Unlocked Labs for giving me a chance and hiring me at a time when most assuredly no-one else would.
I'm also incredibly proud to announce that I am now working for Turso full time, something I would never have dreamed would be possible just a few years ago,

data.title: How to run a shadow library: operations at Anna's Archive (2023)
data.author: the-mitr
data.article_summary: Anna’s Archive是一个致力于建立全球最大开放图书馆的非营利搜索引擎，收录Sci-Hub、Library Genesis和Z-Library等影子图书馆的资源，目标是让知识和文化易于获取，并最终建立一个共同存档和保存全球书籍的社区。运营这样一个具有法律风险的网站面临诸多挑战，包括技术的选择和法律问题。技术上使用简单的Flask、MariaDB和ElasticSearch组合，以避免创新上的过度投入，而将精力集中在规避法律风险。在法律方面，不同国家的版权法不同，有些国家禁止分发或链接到受版权保护的作品，因此网站的合法性视司法管辖区而定。此外，支付方式也受限，只能使用加密货币。为确保网站稳定运行，采用“自由友好”供应商和“廉价供应商”结合的方式，并通过Cloudflare提供额外保护层。网站还实现了自动域名切换功能以应对服务器关闭风险。

Anna’s Blog
Updates about
Anna’s Archive
, the largest truly open library in human history.
How to run a shadow library: operations at Anna’s Archive
annas-archive.li/blog, 2023-03-19
I run
Anna’s Archive
, the world’s largest open-source non-profit search engine for
shadow libraries
, like Sci-Hub, Library Genesis, and Z-Library. Our goal is to make knowledge and culture readily accessible, and ultimately to build a community of people who together archive and preserve
all the books in the world
.
In this article I’ll show how we run this website, and the unique challenges that come with operating a website with questionable legal status, since there is no “AWS for shadow charities”.
Also check out the sister article
How to become a pirate archivist
.
Innovation tokens
Let’s start with our tech stack. It is deliberately boring. We use Flask, MariaDB, and ElasticSearch. That is literally it. Search is largely a solved problem, and we don’t intend to reinvent it. Besides, we have to spend our
innovation tokens
on something else: not being taken down by the authorities.
So how legal or illegal is Anna’s Archive exactly? This mostly depends on the legal jurisdiction. Most countries believe in some form of copyright, which means that people or companies are assigned an exclusive monopoly on certain types of works for a certain period of time. As an aside, at Anna’s Archive we believe while there are some benefits, overall copyright is a net-negative for society — but that is a story for another time.
This exclusive monopoly on certain works means that it is illegal for anyone outside of this monopoly to directly distribute those works — including us. But Anna’s Archive is a search engine that doesn’t directly distribute those works (at least not on our clearnet website), so we should be okay, right? Not exactly. In many jurisdictions it is not only illegal to distribute copyrighted works, but also to link to places that do. A classic example of this is the United States’ DMCA law.
That is the strictest end of the spectrum. On the other end of the spectrum there could theoretically be countries with no copyright laws whatsoever, but these don’t really exist. Pretty much every country has some form of copyright law on the books. Enforcement is a different story. There are plenty of countries with governments that do not care to enforce copyright law. There are also countries in between the two extremes, which prohibit distributing copyrighted works, but do not prohibit linking to such works.
Another consideration is at the company-level. If a company operates in a jurisdiction that doesn’t care about copyright, but the company itself is not willing to take any risk, then they might shut down your website as soon as anyone complains about it.
Finally, a big consideration is payments. Since we need to stay anonymous, we cannot use traditional payment methods. This leaves us with cryptocurrencies, and only a small subset of companies support those (there are virtual debit cards paid by crypto, but they are often not accepted).
System architecture
So let’s say that you found some companies that are willing to host your website without shutting you down — let’s call these “freedom-loving providers” 😄. You’ll quickly find that hosting everything with them is rather expensive, so you might want to find some “cheap providers” and do the actual hosting there, proxying through the freedom-loving providers. If you do it right, the cheap providers will never know what you are hosting, and never receive any complaints.
With all of these providers there is a risk of them shutting you down anyway, so you also need redundancy. We need this on all levels of our stack.
One somewhat freedom-loving company that has put itself in an interesting position is Cloudflare. They have
argued
that they are not a hosting provider, but a utility, like an ISP. They are therefore not subject to DMCA or other takedown requests, and forward any requests to your actual hosting provider. They have gone as far as going to court to protect this structure. We can therefore use them as another layer of caching and protection.
Cloudflare does not accept anonymous payments, so we can only use their free plan. This means that we can’t use their load balancing or failover features. We therefore
implemented this ourselves
at the domain level. On page load, the browser will check if the current domain is still available, and if not, it rewrites all URLs to a different domain. Since Cloudflare caches many pages, this means that a user can land on our main domain, even if the proxy server is down, and then on the next click be moved over to another domain.
We still also have normal operational concerns to deal with, such as monitoring server health, logging backend and frontend errors, and so on. Our failover architecture allows for more robustness on this front as well, for example by running a completely different set of servers on one of the domains. We can
44298849.article_summary: Anna’s Archive是一个致力于建立全球最大开放图书馆的非营利搜索引擎，收录Sci-Hub、Library Genesis和Z-Library等影子图书馆的资源，目标是让知识和文化易于获取，并最终建立一个共同存档和保存全球书籍的社区。运营这样一个具有法律风险的网站面临诸多挑战，包括技术的选择和法律问题。技术上使用简单的Flask、MariaDB和ElasticSearch组合，以避免创新上的过度投入，而将精力集中在规避法律风险。在法律方面，不同国家的版权法不同，有些国家禁止分发或链接到受版权保护的作品，因此网站的合法性视司法管辖区而定。此外，支付方式也受限，只能使用加密货币。为确保网站稳定运行，采用“自由友好”供应商和“廉价供应商”结合的方式，并通过Cloudflare提供额外保护层。网站还实现了自动域名切换功能以应对服务器关闭风险。

data.title: Occurences of swearing in the Linux kernel source code over time
data.author: microsoftedging
data.article_summary: 这篇文章介绍了一个可以分析Linux内核源代码中单词、名称或函数出现频率的工具。用户可以输入自定义的逗号分隔列表进行查询，支持使用`*`作为通配符和`foo|bar`进行求和运算。单词定义为`\<[[:alnum:]_]+\>`，不区分大小写但考虑重音字符。如果启用Javascript，还可以看到交互式图形；否则只能看到过时的静态图片。文章还提到其他有趣内容，包括对咒骂、公司、人物、文件系统、爱与恨、布尔值、64位架构、垃圾、黑客行为、*nix系统和自定义主题的探讨。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：开源代码中使用的语言及其影响，包括脏话、技术术语的跨语言使用以及企业在代码贡献中的表现。

不同观点：
• PaulHoule和sschueller指出，“retarded”在技术领域是一个描述延迟的中性词，而非侮辱性词语。PaulHoule还提到在法语和英语中该词的含义差异，并举例说明如“Couche-Tard”这样的词汇在不同语言环境中的有趣现象。
• holowoodman认为，代码中较少使用脏话可能反映了企业的介入，使得原本充满激情和个性的开源项目变得乏味和一致。
• Pannoniae持相反观点，认为代码中使用脏话表明开发者充满激情，而不是为了简历或企业目的而工作。同时，这种做法有助于筛选出不易被冒犯的人。

补充讨论：
• d3m0t3p讨论了公司（如Meta和IBM）在Linux内核贡献中的表现，通过数据可视化展示了不同公司在贡献量上的变化，并质疑这些名字是否真正代表了实际的代码贡献。
• gwbas1c分享了一个实习经历，通过在源代码树中搜索脏话，来区分专业与非专业的行为。
• RedShift1猜测脏话大多出现在驱动程序和硬件交互部分，暗示这些部分的开发可能更为复杂和压力大。
• b0a04gl进一步分析了企业名字在代码中的出现是否真正反映了其对上游补丁的贡献，并提出需要考虑文件密度和上下文结构。
• egypturnash和bArray通过链接和数据展示了代码中脏话的使用趋势，并讨论了某些词汇（如“ass”和“dumb”）的使用频率上升现象。
• dhsysusbsjsi幽默地表达了对澳大利亚关键脏话“cunt”在图表中缺席的失望。
• tianqi对“garbage”等词汇使用量的增长表示关注，并提出这是否反映了英语的演变。
• f4c39012认为“idiot”是最有害的词汇，可能对积极合作产生负面影响。
• amelius通过链接分享了一个开发者在挫折中做出冒犯性手势的视频，提醒人们注意开发中的情绪管理。

争议焦点：
• 代码中使用脏话是否代表激情和个性，或者是否应被视为不专业的表现。
• 企业介入开源项目是否导致代码变得乏味和一致。
• 不同语言和文化背景下，技术术语的理解差异及其可能引发的误解。

data.title: Linux kernel WireGuard can go 'fast' on decent hardware
data.author: zdw
data.article_summary: 本文解释了为何一些使用旧浏览器版本的用户或通过某些网页档案服务（如archive.*）访问作者博客"Wandering Thoughts"时会被阻止。原因是为应对2025年初大量使用旧浏览器用户代理的高流量爬虫（特别是用于LLM训练），作者实施了反爬虫措施。这些措施可能误伤了合法用户，尤其是通过archive.*网站访问的用户，因为它们的爬取行为与恶意爬虫相似。若访问被误拦，用户可以联系作者并提供浏览器详细信息。作者建议使用更规范的archive.org进行存档访问。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：不同用户对VPN性能及硬件配置的看法

不同观点：
• Octoth0rpe认为WireGuard在消费级WiFi路由器硬件上的表现显著优于OpenVPN，尤其是在升级路由器后，速度提升了5倍。这表明WireGuard在性能上有明显优势。

• Hexmiles补充了WireGuard的另一个优点，即它在处理漫游（roaming）时能够可靠地保持活跃连接，而不会中断连接，这一点是其他VPN可能不具备的。

• Justincormack则认为VPN的加密性能已经很久不是问题了，尤其是对于有硬件支持的AES128加密，其性能应该比WireGuard使用的ChaCha20更快。他提到自己的笔记本电脑可以以2GB/s的速度运行ChaCha20，因此对WireGuard的速度优势持保留态度。

• Lotharcable分享了自己的DIY网络设备经验，通过使用便宜的二手10GbE以太网组件搭建了一个高性能的网络交换机，并成功保持线路速度。虽然没有具体测试WireGuard，但他认为WireGuard应该能有效工作并达到高速度。

补充讨论：
• 用户对VPN性能的关注点不同，有的关注加密算法和硬件加速，有的则关注具体应用场景如漫游和连接稳定性。
• 不同用户通过实际使用经验提供了不同的硬件解决方案和性能优化方法，展现了多样化的技术路径。
• 争议的焦点在于WireGuard是否在所有情况下都显著优于其他VPN方案，尤其是与AES128相比的性能优势。

You're using a suspiciously old browser
You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access
some part of
my blog (Wandering Thoughts)
or
CSpace
, the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately
you're using a browser version that my anti-crawler precautions consider
suspicious, most often because it's too old (most often this applies to
versions of Chrome). Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague
of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM
training) that use a variety of old browser user agents, especially
Chrome user agents. To reduce the load on
Wandering Thoughts
I'm experimenting with
(attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this.
If this is in error and you're using a current version of your
browser of choice, you can contact me at
my current place at the
university
(you should be able to work out the email address
from that). If possible, please let me know what browser you're
using and so on, ideally with its exactl User-Agent string.
A special note for people using archive.*
You may be seeing this through archive.today, archive.ph, archive.is,
and so on. Unfortunately, archive.* crawls pages to archive in a way that
is impossible to distinguish from malicious actors. They use old Chrome
User-Agent values, crawl from IP address blocks that are widely distributed
and not clearly identified as theirs, and some of their IP addresses have
falsified reverse DNS entries that claim they are googlebot IP addresses
(which is something that is normally done only by quite bad actors). I
suggest that you use archive.org, which is a better behaved archival
crawler and can crawl
my blog (Wandering Thoughts)
.
Chris Siebenmann, 2025-02-17
44298369.article_summary: 本文解释了为何一些使用旧浏览器版本的用户或通过某些网页档案服务（如archive.*）访问作者博客"Wandering Thoughts"时会被阻止。原因是为应对2025年初大量使用旧浏览器用户代理的高流量爬虫（特别是用于LLM训练），作者实施了反爬虫措施。这些措施可能误伤了合法用户，尤其是通过archive.*网站访问的用户，因为它们的爬取行为与恶意爬虫相似。若访问被误拦，用户可以联系作者并提供浏览器详细信息。作者建议使用更规范的archive.org进行存档访问。
44298369.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：不同用户对VPN性能及硬件配置的看法

不同观点：
• Octoth0rpe认为WireGuard在消费级WiFi路由器硬件上的表现显著优于OpenVPN，尤其是在升级路由器后，速度提升了5倍。这表明WireGuard在性能上有明显优势。

• Hexmiles补充了WireGuard的另一个优点，即它在处理漫游（roaming）时能够可靠地保持活跃连接，而不会中断连接，这一点是其他VPN可能不具备的。

• Justincormack则认为VPN的加密性能已经很久不是问题了，尤其是对于有硬件支持的AES128加密，其性能应该比WireGuard使用的ChaCha20更快。他提到自己的笔记本电脑可以以2GB/s的速度运行ChaCha20，因此对WireGuard的速度优势持保留态度。

• Lotharcable分享了自己的DIY网络设备经验，通过使用便宜的二手10GbE以太网组件搭建了一个高性能的网络交换机，并成功保持线路速度。虽然没有具体测试WireGuard，但他认为WireGuard应该能有效工作并达到高速度。

补充讨论：
• 用户对VPN性能的关注点不同，有的关注加密算法和硬件加速，有的则关注具体应用场景如漫游和连接稳定性。

data.title: NexusMods Changes Hands
data.author: gmemstr
data.article_summary: Nexus Mods创始人宣布将日常管理交给新领导层，因长期压力和健康问题决定退居幕后。自2001年创立以来，Nexus Mods已成为他的整个成年生活，但他意识到自己精疲力竭，影响了团队和网站发展。经过多方寻找，他找到了理解和尊重模组社区的新 ownership 团队，确保网站的长期稳定和社区至上的价值观不变。创始人在必要时仍会参与指导，但不再负责日常事务，这有利于他和网站的未来发展。新团队包括Victor、Marinus和Nikolai，他们将引领Nexus Mods进入新时代。网站运营和社区支持将保持不变，继续支持模组社区的发展。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Nexus Mods平台的优缺点及其在游戏模组社区中的作用

不同观点：
• [xnorswap] 认为Nexus Mods的体验相对较差，尤其是与其他具有内置模组浏览器的游戏（如Factorio）或社区自建的开源模组平台（如KSP的CKAN）相比。他希望更多开发者能提供更好的模组管理体验。
• [zeagle] 承认Nexus Mods在过去提供了重要的服务，尤其是在带宽昂贵时的集中存储库。但他对某些游戏（如Oblivion和Fallout New Vegas）的模组数量不足感到失望，并提到自己花费大量时间配置模组却没时间玩游戏。此外，他还提到Nexus在安全方面的表现（如数据泄露）。
• [orthoxerox] 批评Nexus Mods平台对某些模组的审查，认为它屏蔽了一些仅对字符串或标志纹理做轻微修改的模组，违背了分享模组的初衷。
• [brianjlogan] 对Nexus Mods持积极态度，认为它为像他这样的普通玩家提供了便捷的模组安装体验，尤其是在没有模组管理器的年代。他表示，尽管Nexus无法让所有人满意，但它对他的游戏体验有着重要影响。
• [strangescript] 对那些批评Nexus Mods尝试做模组合集的人表示不满，认为这些人对Nexus Mods有过高的控制欲和期望，而Nexus Mods作为一个免费平台已经提供了很多。
• [zelphirkalt] 认为Nexus平台的用户体验较差，注册和登录过程繁琐，希望未来能简化流程，让用户专注于下载模组本身。

补充讨论：
• Nexus Mods在过去提供了重要的服务，特别是在带宽昂贵时的集中存储库，但随着时间推移，用户对其体验的评价出现分歧。
• 争议的焦点包括平台对模组的审查、用户体验（如登录和注册过程）、以及平台在模组社区中的角色和控制。
• 一些用户对Nexus Mods的贡献表示感谢，而另一些用户则对其管理方式和用户体验感到不满。
• 安全问题也被提及，如数据泄露。

44296835.article_content:
After almost 24 years of running Nexus Mods, the time has come for me to step back from the day-to-day management of the site. This isn't a decision I've made lightly - far from it - but one I think is in both my and the community's best interests.
I started this project back in 2001, in my bedroom, with a 56k modem, an excitement for the upcoming release of Morrowind and with no grand ambitions or intentions. I didn’t set out to build a business, I just wanted to make a place where modders could share their work without worrying it would vanish into the internet either the next time a fansite went offline or a publisher decided they were done with it. That idea grew legs, sprouted arms, and turned into Nexus Mods.
Since then, this site has been my entire adult life. Every single day, for over two decades, I’ve been "on call", whether it was fixing issues, reading feedback, pushing updates, or getting pulled into the latest bit of community drama. It’s been rewarding, sometimes chaotic, often exhausting and always personal. Somewhere along the way, I forgot to step back and breathe, or sleep properly. The dilemma of running a major social network that does not rest!
The strain of being responsible for the behemoth I created has taken its toll. The stress of the job has been a regular source of anxiety and stress-related health issues. I realised that I have been burning out and this started to have an impact on my staff and Nexus Mods as a whole. So, I firmly believe that the best thing for the future of Nexus Mods is for me to step aside and bring in new leadership to steer the business forward with renewed energy to make Nexus Mods the modding community we all truly deserve.
One of the biggest reasons I've been doing this for so long is that I've never felt that I truly found someone who really "gets" the modding community the way I do. Finding a new owner who would be able to understand and respect the myriad intricacies of both Nexus Mods as a business and the wider modding community was essential.
After months of meetings, face-to-face talks, and a whole lot of soul searching, I am thrilled to say that I truly believe I have found the exact right people for the task.
So yes, the ownership of Nexus Mods has changed hands, but I want to be clear, this isn’t some corporate “exit” or a backroom deal. This is me doing something I probably should’ve done years ago: taking care of myself. Reclaiming some headspace. And finally letting go of the idea that I have to do everything and be responsible for everything myself.
What changes now?
Honestly, not a lot, at least not from your side of things.
Behind the scenes, I’ve already been stepping back bit by bit. Over the past few years, the team has taken on more of the weight and the site’s been doing better than ever. What’s changing now is simply the formality of it, making sure the right people are in place to guide Nexus Mods into the next era.
That includes some structural updates to the company ownership that we aren’t shouting about, but I want to be transparent: they’re about long-term stability, not changing the values or direction of the platform. Nexus Mods is community-first and mod-author focused, that’s not up for negotiation.
While I am stepping back, it's important to understand that Nexus Mods isn't just about me and hasn't been for a long time. The Nexus Mods you see today has been created by a team of 40 incredibly dedicated people, some of whom have been here for over 9 years. They live and breathe modding, they care deeply, they’re experienced, committed, and they're very much still here. None of that is changing.
So if I can ask one thing, it’s to continue supporting them, the site, and the community they help nurture every day.
In terms of new faces, you’ll also be seeing more of
Foledinho
(Victor),
Rapsak
(Marinus) and
Taagen
(Nikolai), who’ve come on board to lead this next chapter. They’ve got deep roots in gaming, tech, and most importantly, they give a damn; about the site, the community, and the future we’re trying to build here.
Editor's Note: We've added Nikolai to the new owners listed above. He works more in the background, but is still an important part of the team!
They have my complete trust, and I’m incredibly proud to be bringing them onboard.
What about me?
I’m not disappearing. I’ll still be annoying people on the Mod Author Discord, lurking on the forums, and sticking my nose into community matters when I can’t help myself. I’ll also be working with the team to help guide the overall direction of the site, just without needing to be the person who signs off on every little thing and without taking responsibility for any and all things Nexus Mods.
Frankly, that’s a good thing, for me, for the team, and for the future of Nexus Mods.

data.title: Google aims to reinvent email with Wave (2009)
data.author: xattt
data.article_summary: Google于2009年宣布推出Wave，旨在重新发明21世纪的电子邮件。Wave结合了电子邮件、即时通讯、博客、维基和公告板的功能，提供一种全新的沟通方式。与传统电子邮件不同，Wave支持实时编辑和多人同时在线修改内容，每个按键输入都即时可见，加快了交流速度。Wave还支持文件拖放添加、历史回放功能，以及将整个对话嵌入博客或网页中。此外，开发者可以编写扩展应用，如在Wave中进行国际象棋或数独游戏。Wave的自然语言处理功能还提供了创新的拼写检查。尽管Wave试图整合多种工具，但其核心目标是简化协作和沟通。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Google Wave的成败原因及功能分析

不同观点：
• Wave是一个超前于时代的产品，用户当时无法理解其价值。即使在多年后，人们仍然难以准确分类Wave，有人称其为社交网络、邮件终结者或聊天应用，但实际上它是一个原生的实时协作平台。（[xnx]）
• Wave的邀请机制和供应不足导致其难以在用户中广泛推广，特别是在教育环境中，这成为了一个严重的限制。（[angry_moose]）
• Wave的设计过于复杂，尤其是其实时编辑和显示输入过程的功能，让一些用户感到不适，特别是那些习惯于编辑信息后再发送的用户。（[hbn]）
• Wave失败的一个主要原因是缺乏承诺的功能（如将Wave嵌入网页），并且在发布后几乎没有更新，导致用户无法充分利用其潜力。（[Apreche]）
• 一些用户非常欣赏Wave的实时互动功能，认为这种即时性和协作性在其他应用中难以找到。（[jap], [tzury], [jdmg94], [thendrill]）

补充讨论：
• Wave在个人和团队项目管理中展现了巨大的潜力，甚至有人基于Wave构建了项目管理系统，但Google过早地放弃了该项目。（[tzury], [mark_l_watson]）
• 一些用户对Wave的消亡表示遗憾，并指出即使在开源后，也难以让朋友和家人使用它。（[mark_l_watson]）
• 有评论认为Google当时过于追求立即成功，如果以同样的态度对待现在的LLM（大语言模型），Google可能会错失领先机会。（[strangescript]）
• 对于没有使用过Wave的用户来说，他们好奇Wave提供了哪些当前产品仍未实现的功能。（[esafak]）

争议焦点：
• Wave的实时编辑和显示输入过程的功能被一部分用户赞赏，认为增加了互动性，但另一部分用户则认为这让他们感到不适和压力。（[jap], [hbn]）
• Wave的复杂性和超前性是否是其失败的主要原因存在不同看法，一部分用户认为如果Google持续更新和迭代，Wave有可能成功。（[Apreche], [strangescript]）

44298081.article_content:
Canada
How Google aims to reinvent email with Wave
Google wants to reinvent email for the 21st century. What's new in Wave?
Google wants to reinvent email for the 21st century. What's new in Wave?
John Bowman
·
CBC News
·
Posted: Jul 27, 2009 1:30 PM EDT | Last Updated: October 1, 2009
Social Sharing
Google Wave's inbox, as seen on the Official Google Blog.
((Courtesy Google))
In May, Google announced Wave, the company's attempt to reinvent internet communication. Brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen, the Australian creators of Google Maps, have been working on the project for the last two years.
On Sept. 30, Google opened its preview of Wave beyond the 6,000 or so software developers who are currently helping to build the service. About 100,000 users can now see what Wave is all about.
Google Wave incorporates ideas from email, instant messaging, blogs, wikis and bulletin boards into a single new method of communicating. But we already have email, IM, wikis and the rest, so why do we need one tool that does all of these things? What is new in Google Wave?
How old is email?
The online tools you use every day might be older than you think. (Like everything on the internet, the date of origin of these tools is up for debate.)
Email/instant messaging: 1965
Bulletin Board Systems: 1978
Newsgroups: 1979
Internet: 1983
World Wide Web: 1989
Search engines: 1990
Web browsers: 1991
Wikis: 1995
VoIP: 1995
Blogs: 1997
Social networking sites: 1997
Microblogs (e.g. Twitter): 2006
Live editing by multiple users
In their first demo of Wave at the Google I/O conference, the project's lead engineer, Lars Rasmussen, and project manager Stephanie Hannon demonstrated how a conversation that starts out looking like an email, with replies going back and forth, can turn seamlessly into an instant messaging conversation if more than one person has the wave open at the same time.
Actually, the conversation is even more instant than instant messaging. Each key stroke by every participant in the wave is visible to all the others as it occurs. Rasmussen said this would result in faster communication than IM because you wouldn't be spending half the conversation waiting for the other person to hit "Enter."
However, he seemed to recognize that not everyone would want to communicate in this way, and said that a wave's settings could be changed so that messages are only sent after the user hits "Enter."
This live communication isn't limited to IM-type conversations. Anything in a wave can be edited by anyone who's been invited into it, including the original message. In the demo, colour-coded cursors, labelled with their owners' names, race around a document, all making changes simultaneously.
Playback
You can add people to a wave at any time, in much the same way you can forward an email. But someone coming into a wave after three other people have discussed and collaborated on a document might not see right away how the conversation went.
To address this, each wave has controls to move back and forth through time to see all the changes to the wave in the order they happened. Every wave stores the history of changes that have been made to it, in same the way a page on Wikipedia has a history, making the playback possible.
Drag-and-drop adding of files
Instead of attaching files as you would in an email, you can drag and drop files directly into a wave conversation. Google Wave's Stephanie Hannon showed how several people could contribute to a group photo album by dragging and dropping the files from the desktop into a wave. (She pointed out that HTML 5 doesn't yet support this function, and it required a browser plug-in called Gears to work.)
Dropping Word documents, spreadsheets or slide presentations into a wave could make collaborating on a project simpler than email, where tracking different versions of such documents can be challenging.
Embedding
A wave can be embedded on to a blog post (or any web page) in the same way a Google Map can. Changes made to the wave are immediately seen in the embedded version. In this way, a wave can act like a comments section on a blog post or a web-based chat room. A photo gallery created by you and your friends can be posted on your blog for everyone to see.
A sudoku game being played inside Google Wave. (Courtesy Google)
Extensions and applications
Developers can write their own applications that run inside Google Wave, in the same way that third-party applications run inside Facebook. In the demo, Wave's developers showed how a chess game would unfold inside a wave, complete with the playback feature to show each move in order.
A Sudoku game inside a wave becomes a competition to see who can fill in the most squares correctly. And because the team behind Wave also built Google Maps, they showed off a Maps gadget that allows two or more people to mark locations on the same map at the same time.

• Wave的复杂性和超前性是否是其失败的主要原因存在不同看法，一部分用户认为如果Google持续更新和迭代，Wave有可能成功。（[Apreche], [strangescript]）

data.title: Insanity: Locked Out (2020)
data.author: theandrewbailey
data.article_summary: 这篇文章讲述了一位极度忠实的谷歌粉丝，深陷谷歌生态系统，甚至搬进了谷歌打造的智能社区。在这个高度互联的“科技乌托邦”中，一切由传感器和人工智能控制，生活极其便利。然而，一次由于违反服务条款，他被系统锁定，无法进入自己的公寓，所有设备也失效。求助无门后，他试图用原始工具解决问题，但失败了。最终，他在愤怒中毁坏了社区设备，被警方逮捕，面临多项法律指控。文章讽刺了对科技巨头过度依赖的生活，以及在高度数字化社会中失去个人控制权的风险。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：用户对Google及其服务的可靠性存在质疑，特别是关于关键任务和客户支持的问题。

不同观点：
• **gloosx的观点**：不信任Google处理关键任务，强调需要有应急计划和备份。他分享了自己的负面体验：在Google Pixel手机上更改国家设置时遇到功能失效，且Google客服没有回复其支持请求。这表明他对Google服务的技术问题和客服支持非常不满。

• **gamegod的观点**：通过分享一篇关于Sidewalk Labs建筑的文章，似乎暗示Google或其相关项目（如Sidewalk Labs）在实际运营中遇到困难或失败。虽然没有明确表达立场，但通过分享文章引发对Google项目可持续性的质疑。

• **theamk的观点**：仅提到“Needs (2018)”，可能是在暗示2018年有类似的需求或问题未得到解决，或在指出Google服务的问题并非新近发生，而是一直存在。虽然没有详细说明，但可能是在呼应gloosx对Google长期存在问题的担忧。

补充讨论：
- **技术问题**：gloosx具体指出了Google Pixel手机中Play Store的“更改国家”功能失效，且没有错误提示，表明Google产品在技术实现上存在缺陷。
- **客户支持问题**：gloosx提到提交支持请求后未收到回复，显示出对Google客户服务的不满。
- **项目可持续性**：gamegod分享的Sidewalk Labs链接暗示Google的一些大型项目可能面临失败或质疑，进一步加剧了对Google可靠性的担忧。
- **历史问题**：theamk的评论暗示Google的问题可能并非新近发生，而是一直存在，提示用户需要长期保持警惕。

争议焦点：Google服务在处理关键任务时的可靠性以及其客户支持的有效性。

44297882.article_content:
Imagine that you're a loyal Google fanboy. You've had an Android phone in your pocket for as long as you can remember, and buy a new one every 8 months (at least). You believe that other search engines don't work. You died a bit when Buzz and Reader were killed, but you bought the rationale behind it. If a video isn't on YouTube, you don't watch it. You stood in line overnight for Google Glass, Google Home, and every Nexus device. You faithfully attend most Google conferences and product launches, live Plussing them on your Chromebook (to the annoyance of your friends), followed by an in-depth Blogger post. When you see a non-Google advertisement, or someone not using Chrome, you retreat to your brightly colored safe space.
When you heard that Google was building a neighborhood
, you remembered where you were. Your life changed. It felt like you found the promised land, and were the 937th person that immediately signed up to live there. You've drank so much of the kool-aid, you're almost swimming in it,
and now you want to live in a more physicalized bubble
.
Soon (a few years later), you move into the techno utopia
(beta version)
of your dreams. Sensors are embedded into every surface, to make sure things are "just right". Google's knowledge of you guarantees you will never see a non-Google or unrelevant ad again. You get served food that hits the spot every time. Since you work from home, shop from home, and all the "best" restaurants and venues are within walking distance, you don't need Maps anymore. Your cat eventually gets used to the self cleaning Nest litter box. Robotic trash cans sense that you're eating a candy bar while walking in the park, so one will open and follow you around like a puppy until you've finished your snack and given it a treat (the wrapper). You're living the best life possible!
But one day, you come back to your apartment. It's locked, and won't accept your authentication method.
Since your technocrat landlords despise plain old metal keys for some reason (What are you, a peasant?), they provide one of several alternative methods for you to open doors.
(Why can't those cyborgs be more like normal people?) They advise you to never share how or with what you use to login to them. Whatever it is, it's not working. You hope there's not an electrical outage somewhere: a friend had one of those happen to her and she almost died from the anxiety! (Someone across the room from her wasn't so lucky!) She's still going to therapy for it!
Because you're living in the future, everything is connected to the internet. Like most everything else, your door has a display mounted into it. A message appears, informing you that since you've violated the terms of service, your account has been terminated.
You're locked out from all your stuff!
There is a customer service robot downstairs, so you try to get some answers from it. Unsurprisingly, the robot is not helpful, not sympathetic,
and it won't listen to an unperson
.
You step outside and ponder why on Google's green Earth would you be locked out like this. It's probably something you said or typed, but you're not sure of exactly what. You're a good little fanboy, and every fiber of your being is progressive.
Maybe it was someone you knew.
Taking off your tinfoil hat, you figure that it's probably the local e-lord wanting to have some fun.
After living on the street for 15 minutes, you remember that a friend
sold hammers made out of roots
(or something) in the store. A few months ago, you heard of someone using one of those to get into his stuff. In desperation, you go to the store, but there's none there. You try to open a Hangout with that friend, but your phone is locked, too. It's very hard, but you remember where this guy hangs out in reality.
When you catch up to him, he said that he sold that side project to someone else months ago
, but Google eventually
stopped selling the hammer, because it didn't have a good enough description or pictures
.
While walking around town, considering your options, you pass by someone trying to give away her Google Home, but no one is biting,
because it's one of those big old ones
. She upgraded to the crumb-sized Home
Femto
. (So cute!) You gladly take the big one. You return to your former apartment building, and give that robot a piece of your mind. You relish both the robot and the Home asking you in identical soothing voices to stop. The cops arrive about 10 minutes later,
long after you've bashed both of them to pieces like they were fascists
, scratched your hands and arms in the process, and passed out at the sight of your own blood.
You were charged, not with something like trespassing or vandalism, but
under dozens of charges of the CFAA
, because
no one owns anything anymore
.
(You are merely licensed to use things, because you think that owning things is for chumps.)
You misused both the Home and the robot (2 charges), heard their requests to stop (9 more), failed to obey said requests (9 more)

data.title: How the little-known 'dark roof' lobby may be making US cities hotter
data.author: PaulHoule
data.article_summary: 2010年8月19日，志愿者在纽约布朗克斯为一个屋顶涂上具有高太阳反射率和红外发射率的特殊涂料。这种反光屋顶可以降低城市温度并节省能源，但暗色屋顶制造商正悄然游说阻止相关新规。2025年，田纳西州废除商用建筑必须使用反光屋顶的规定，共和党议员Rusty Grills称此举是为增加消费者选择。批评者警告，这将导致更高的能源成本和更多的热相关疾病。科学表明，浅色屋顶在炎热天气下温度比深色屋顶低50度以上，有助于减少能源使用和温室气体排放。至少八个州和十几个城市已采用反光屋顶要求，但行业团体质疑其科学依据，并反对全国统一标准。随着全球变暖，屋顶已成为气候战争的关键战场。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：城市规划中的热上升气流及其环境影响，特别是对不同区域和人群的影响是否公平。

不同观点：
• 观点一：有人（如squircle）认为，虽然强热上升气流本身可能没有错，但需要证明这种由市场驱动的、自上而下的城市规划方式不会将熵（即无序和环境负担）转嫁给其他人或地区。评论者质疑当前的规划方式是否忽视了我们彼此之间的相互联系，以及这种规划对不同人群的影响是否公平。他们特别提到，不应让某些群体（如其他人的孩子）承受环境负担，而自己却置身事外。

• 观点二：隐含的对立观点可能是默认当前的城市规划和市场驱动的方式是可接受的，且没有显著的环境不公问题。虽然没有明确表述，但从squircle的评论中可以看出，他们反对这种立场，认为有必要质疑和检验当前的做法是否在环境和社会责任方面存在问题。

补充讨论：
• Squircle通过对比在阴凉公园和沥青停车场中的温度差异，指出了不同城市区域的热环境差异，这可能是由城市设计和材料选择导致的。评论者质疑是否有人研究并证明了这种设计不会对环境或某些群体造成不公。

• 评论还提到了生物区域主义（bioregional sense）的概念，这表明在城市规划中应更多考虑环境和生态因素，并质疑当前以市场为主导的规划是否忽视了这些因素。

争议焦点：当前市场驱动的城市规划是否在无形中加剧了环境不公，将某些负面影响（如热上升气流和环境负担）转嫁给特定区域或弱势群体，而受益者却不必承担相应后果。这涉及到环境正义和城市设计中的公平性问题。

Volunteers paint a rooftop with a specialized coating material that has a high solar reflectivity and infrared emissivity, in the Bronx, New York, on 19 August 2010
Photograph: Ken Cavanagh/Alamy
View image in fullscreen
Volunteers paint a rooftop with a specialized coating material that has a high solar reflectivity and infrared emissivity, in the Bronx, New York, on 19 August 2010
Photograph: Ken Cavanagh/Alamy
Floodlight
Climate crisis
How the little-known ‘dark roof’ lobby may be making US cities hotter
As cities heat up, reflective roofs could lower energy bills and help the climate. But dark-roofing manufacturers are waging a quiet campaign to block new rules
This story is co-published with
Floodlight
Ames Alexander of Floodlight
Sun 1 Jun 2025 06.55 EDT
Last modified on Sun 1 Jun 2025 13.54 EDT
Share
It began with a lobbyist’s pitch.
The Tennessee representative Rusty Grills says the lobbyist proposed a simple idea: repeal the state’s requirement for reflective roofs on many commercial buildings.
In late March, Grills and his fellow lawmakers voted to eliminate the rule, scrapping a measure meant to save energy, lower temperatures and protect Tennesseans from extreme heat.
Grills, a Republican, told Floodlight that he introduced the bill to give consumers more choice.
It was another win for a well-organized lobbying campaign led by manufacturers of dark roofing materials.
Industry representatives called the rollback in Tennessee a needed correction as more of the state moved into a hotter climate zone, expanding the reach of the state’s cool-roof rule. Critics called it dangerous and “deceptive”.
“The new law will lead to higher energy costs and greater heat-related illnesses and deaths,” state representative Harold Love and the Rev Jon Robinson said in a statement.
It will, critics warned, make Nashville, Memphis and other cities hotter – particularly in underserved Black and Latino communities, where many struggle to pay their utility bills. Similar lobbying has played out in Denver and Baltimore and at the national level.
Industry groups have questioned the decades-old science behind cool roofs, downplayed the benefits and warned of reduced choice and unintended consequences. “A one-size-fits-all approach doesn’t consider climate variation across different regions,” wrote Ellen Thorp, the executive director of the EPDM Roofing Association, a DC-based national group that represents an industry built primarily on dark materials.
View image in fullscreen
Rusty Grills in Nashville in 2023.
Photograph: George Walker IV/AP
But the weight of the scientific evidence is clear: on hot days, light-colored roofs can stay more than 50 degrees cooler than dark ones, helping cut energy use, curb greenhouse gas emissions and reduce heat-related illnesses and deaths. One
recent study
found that reflective roofs could have saved the lives of more than 240 people who died in London’s 2018 heatwave.
At least eight states – and more than a dozen cities in other states – have adopted cool-roof requirements, according to the
Smart Surfaces Coalition
, a national group of public health and environmental groups that promote reflective roofs, trees and other solutions to make cities healthier.
Industry representatives lobbied successfully in recent months against expanding cool roof recommendations in national professional energy efficiency codes – the standards that many cities and states use to set building regulations.
The stakes are high. As global temperatures rise and heatwaves
grow more deadly
, roofs have become battlefields in a consequential climate war. It’s happening as the Trump administration and Congress
move to derail
measures designed to make appliances and buildings more energy efficient.
Why roof color matters
The principle is simple: light-colored roofs reflect sunlight, so buildings stay cooler. Dark ones absorb heat, driving up temperatures inside buildings and in the surrounding air.
Roofs comprise up to one-fourth of the surface area of major US cities, researchers say, so the color of roofs can make a big difference in urban areas.
Just how hot can dark roofs get?
“You can physically burn your hands on these roofs,” said Bill Updike, who used to install solar panels and now works for the Smart Surfaces Coalition.
Study after study has confirmed the benefits of light-colored roofs. They save energy, lower air-conditioning bills and reduce city temperatures. They help prevent heat-related illnesses. And they typically cost no more than dark roofs.
A
study
by the US Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that a cool roof on a home in central California saved 20% in annual energy costs.
View image in fullscreen
A researcher from the Berkeley lab perform tests on cooling materials.
Photograph: Thor Swift/Berkeley Lab
In a three-story rowhouse in Baltimore, Owen Henry discovered what a difference a cool roof can make.

data.title: Chemical knowledge and reasoning of large language models vs. chemist expertise
data.author: bookofjoe
data.article_summary: 本文介绍了一种名为ChemBench的自动化框架，用于评估大型语言模型（LLMs）在化学知识和推理能力方面与化学专家的对比表现。研究收集了超过2,700个问答对，评估了多种开放和封闭源的LLMs，发现顶级模型在平均表现上优于人类化学家。然而，这些模型在处理某些基本任务时仍显不足，并且常常给出过于自信的预测。研究结果展示了LLMs在化学领域的强大潜力，但同时也强调了进一步研究以提高其安全性和实用性的必要性。此外，本文建议调整化学教育，并强调了在特定领域评估LLMs的基准框架的价值。最后，文章也关注了LLMs在化学安全方面的潜在风险和误用问题。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：大型语言模型（LLM）在化学及其他专业领域（如计算机科学、编程等）中的应用与局限

不同观点：
• PlasmonOwl（化学家的视角）：LLM在化学领域表现不佳，因为化学研究依赖于实践经验和直觉，而这些是LLM不具备的。化学家通过长期的研究积累直觉，而LLM只能处理表面的、记忆性的知识，无法胜任复杂的化学研究任务。例如，化学中的颜色变化可能意味着实验反应的成败，而LLM无法通过简单的提问理解这些细微的实验现象。

• calibas（计算机科学视角）：LLM在计算机科学领域表现优异，因为它们可以快速学习大量的知识，尽管这些知识的深度有限。LLM可以掌握许多编程语言，包括一些冷门的语言，但它们在专业领域上仍然难以超越专注于该领域的人类专家。

• 6LLvveMx2koXfwn（对同行评审制度的反思）：评论指出了同行评审期刊文章在快速发展领域中的局限性，暗示这种出版模式可能已经过时。

A framework for evaluating the chemical knowledge and reasoning abilities of large language models against the expertise of chemists
Download PDF
Download PDF
Subjects
Chemical safety
Cheminformatics
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have gained widespread interest owing to their ability to process human language and perform tasks on which they have not been explicitly trained. However, we possess only a limited systematic understanding of the chemical capabilities of LLMs, which would be required to improve models and mitigate potential harm. Here we introduce ChemBench, an automated framework for evaluating the chemical knowledge and reasoning abilities of state-of-the-art LLMs against the expertise of chemists. We curated more than 2,700 question–answer pairs, evaluated leading open- and closed-source LLMs and found that the best models, on average, outperformed the best human chemists in our study. However, the models struggle with some basic tasks and provide overconfident predictions. These findings reveal LLMs’ impressive chemical capabilities while emphasizing the need for further research to improve their safety and usefulness. They also suggest adapting chemistry education and show the value of benchmarking frameworks for evaluating LLMs in specific domains.

data.article_summary: 亚历山大·波波夫（Oleksandr Popov）1967年出生于基辅，父亲是计算机科学家，母亲是演员，这种科技与艺术的双重背景深刻影响了他的艺术视野。童年时常随父亲接触早期苏联计算机，并在母亲指导下学习表演。1975至1983年，他在基辅数学与计算机专科学校表现出色，14岁时制作了简易的互动“算命机”。1982年，发表关于早期聊天机器人概念的论文。1983年，入读明斯克理工学院，但对僵化的课程失望，转而加入地下计算机团体“Elektronika”，开发兼具游戏和心理实验性质的程序。1986年，与团体理念分歧后创立“PopovSoft Ltd”，开发多款实验性软件，包括引发心理效应的“Labirint Razuma”和24小时实验程序“Ispytaniye”。1988年，辍学投身行为艺术，结束PopovSoft Ltd。波波夫的创作始终探索技术与意识的本质。

Alexander Popov — Biographical Timeline
“The experience continues until you stop experiencing it.”
1967
Born in Kyiv, Ukraine (then Ukrainian SSR) as Oleksandr Mykhailo Popov
. His father, Dr. Mikhail Popov, was a respected computer scientist at the
V.M. Glushkov Institute of Cybernetics
of the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) of Ukraine, working on early artificial intelligence systems and cybernetic theory. His mother, Lyudmila Popova (née Kovalenko), was a prominent actress with the Lesya Ukrainka National Academic Theater. This dual heritage of cutting-edge technology and theatrical performance would profoundly shape his artistic vision.
1970-1975
As a child, frequently accompanies his father to the Glushkov Institute, where he is exposed to the
MESM (Small Electronic Calculating Machine)
and other early Soviet computers. Institute colleagues recall a precocious boy who would ask sophisticated questions about machine logic and human-computer interaction. At home, his mother trains him in voice, movement, and dramatic presentation, treating their apartment as an informal theater studio.
1975-1983
Attends the specialized
School No. 145 for mathematics and computer science in Kyiv
, showing remarkable aptitude for both programming and electronics. Creates his first rudimentary interactive experience at age 14, combining a reprogrammed calculator, tape recorder, and homemade electronic circuits to create a “fortune-telling machine” that responded differently based on how users interacted with it. His teachers note his unusual interest in the psychological effects of human-computer interaction.
1982
While still in school, publishes a paper in a youth science journal detailing an algorithm for generating “conversational responses that create the illusion of understanding,” essentially an early chatbot concept. The paper includes philosophical questions about the nature of consciousness and reality that seem advanced for his age
1983
Following his father’s connections and recommendations, moves to Minsk to attend the prestigious
Belarusian Polytechnic Institute
(now Belarusian National Technical University) to study computer engineering. His professors initially have high expectations due to his father’s reputation in Soviet computing circles.
1984
Becomes increasingly disenchanted with the rigid technical curriculum. Finds an intellectual home in the underground “Elektronika” collective, a secret group of students and young engineers creating unofficial games and programs for Soviet computers like the
Elektronika BK-0010
and
MK-61 programmable calculators
. The group eventually acquires smuggled Commodore 64 systems through Polish connections, opening Alexander’s eyes to Western game design.
1985
While maintaining adequate academic performance, devotes increasing time to the Elektronika collective. Develops a reputation for creating programs that blur the line between games and psychological experiments. Creates “Dialog s Neznakomtsem” (Dialogue with a Stranger), a text-based program that asks increasingly personal questions and responds in ways designed to create emotional attachment to the computer.
1986
Has philosophical falling out with the Elektronika collective over the purpose of computing. While most members are interested in replicating Western gaming experiences, Popov argues for creating “new realities that question the nature of consciousness.” Leaves the group and establishes “PopovSoft Ltd,” an ironically named one-person “company” that becomes his publishing identity for increasingly experimental software.
1986-1987
Under the PopovSoft Ltd label, develops several boundary-pushing programs including “Kosmos-3” (a space simulation with philosophical elements) and his most significant early work, “Labirint Razuma” (Labyrinth of the Mind). This latter program combines mathematical puzzles with existential questions and was distributed on magnetic tapes throughout the Soviet computing underground. Users reported strange psychological effects after prolonged interaction with the program, establishing Popov’s early interest in altered states of consciousness through technology.
1987
Creates the controversial “Ispytaniye” (The Test), his most technically sophisticated program for the
Elektronika BK-0010
. Designed to run for exactly 24 hours, it requires participants to interact with it at specific intervals, tracking whether they are following instructions even when not at the computer. The few who completed the full cycle reported experiencing “a profound shift in perception.” Computer historians later note similarities between this work and his later physical installations.
1988
Abandons his studies at the Polytechnic Institute after becoming disillusioned with the rigid Soviet educational system. Begins experimenting with performance art, staging small happenings that combine technology and audience participation. • [troelsSteegin] 对文章表示欣赏，并提出了进一步的思考。他认为在将系统范围的信息提供给个体代理时，模型需要考虑代理的信息处理能力，比如注意力或分析预算。他进一步指出，信息的不对称性不仅仅在于信息的获取，还在于信息的解读。
